claim: Sirtuins are NAD+-dependent deacetylases present in all forms of life.
source: Sirtuins are NAD+-dependent deacetylases that are present in all forms of life.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about sirtuins cited from the literature (Landry et al., 2000).

claim: Sirtuins remove acetyl moiety from lysine residues of proteins in the presence of NAD+ as a cofactor.
source: Sirtuins comprise a conserved core catalytic domain that removes acetyl moiety from the lysine residues of proteins in the presence of NAD+ as a cofactor (Landry et al., 2000), giving rise to 2'O-acetyl-ADP-ribose and free nicotinamide as products (Jackson and Denu, 2002; Sauve et al., 2001).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by citations to published research (Landry et al., 2000; Jackson and Denu, 2002; Sauve et al., 2001).

claim: Free nicotinamide acts as a non-competitive inhibitor of sirtuins.
source: Free nicotinamide acts as a non-competitive inhibitor of sirtuins (Bitterman et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bitterman et al., 2002.

claim: Mammals have seven sirtuins that regulate various biological functions such as cell survival, apoptosis, oxidative stress, metabolism, and inflammation.
source: Mammals have seven sirtuins that are responsible for regulating various biological functions such as cell survival, apoptosis, oxidative stress, metabolism, and inflammation (Lin and Fang, 2013; Guarente, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Lin and Fang, 2013; Guarente, 2007).

claim: SIRT1, 6, and 7 have nuclear localization.
source: SIRT1, 6, and 7 have nuclear localization, SIRT2 is cytoplasmic, and SIRT 3, 4, and 5 comprise the mitochondrial SIRTs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sirtuin subcellular localization.

claim: SIRT2 is cytoplasmic.
source: SIRT1, 6, and 7 have nuclear localization, SIRT2 is cytoplasmic, and SIRT 3, 4, and 5 comprise the mitochondrial SIRTs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sirtuin subcellular localization.

claim: SIRT 3, 4, and 5 comprise the mitochondrial SIRTs.
source: SIRT1, 6, and 7 have nuclear localization, SIRT2 is cytoplasmic, and SIRT 3, 4, and 5 comprise the mitochondrial SIRTs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sirtuin subcellular localization.

claim: SIRT1 gets activated in response to acute immune response and deacetylates RelA/p65 component of NFκB, thereby mediating its proteasomal degradation.
source: Previous studies have shown that SIRT1 gets activated in response to acute immune response and deacetylates RelA/p65 component of NFκB, thereby mediating its proteasomal degradation (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2011.

claim: SIRT1 activates RelB component of NFκB pathway.
source: On the other hand, it activates RelB component of NFκB pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the text following the previous claim about SIRT1 and p65.

claim: RelB causes heterochromatinization of pro-inflammatory genes like Tnfa and Il1b.
source: RelB causes heterochromatinization of pro-inflammatory genes like Tnfa and Il1b (El Gazzar et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to El Gazzar et al., 2007.

claim: SIRT1 activates peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ (PPARγ) coactivator-1α (PGC-1α), mediating a metabolic switch from glycolysis toward fatty acid oxidation (FAO).
source: SIRT1 activates peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ (PPARγ) coactivator-1α (PGC-1α), mediating a metabolic switch from glycolysis toward fatty acid oxidation (FAO).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: SIRT1-mediated RelB activation activates SIRT3, causing the promotion of mitochondrial bioenergetics.
source: SIRT1-mediated RelB activation, in turn, activates SIRT3, causing the promotion of mitochondrial bioenergetics (Liu et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2015b.

claim: PGC-1α activates SIRT3.
source: PGC-1α, a major player in mitochondrial biogenesis, activates SIRT3 (Kong et al., 2010), which in turn causes activation of PGC-1α, thereby fuelling a positive feedback loop.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kong et al., 2010.

claim: SIRT3 causes activation of PGC-1α, thereby fuelling a positive feedback loop.
source: PGC-1α, a major player in mitochondrial biogenesis, activates SIRT3 (Kong et al., 2010), which in turn causes activation of PGC-1α, thereby fuelling a positive feedback loop.
evidence: This is stated in the text following the citation to Kong et al., 2010.

claim: SIRT3 accounts for the major mitochondrial deacetylase, orchestrating several metabolic processes such as fatty acid oxidation (FAO), promotion of the Tricaroboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, and inhibition of Reactive oxygen species (ROS) production.
source: SIRT3 accounts for the major mitochondrial deacetylase, orchestrating several metabolic processes such as fatty acid oxidation (FAO), promotion of the Tricaroboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, and inhibition of Reactive oxygen species (ROS) production (van de Ven et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to van de Ven et al., 2017.

claim: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium is a facultative intracellular Gram-negative enteric pathogen, causing a wide array of infections ranging from self-limiting gastroenteritis to diarrhoea in humans.
source: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium is a facultative intracellular Gram-negative enteric pathogen, causing a wide array of infections ranging from self-limiting gastroenteritis to diarrhoea in humans (Garai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to Garai et al., 2012.

claim: S. enterica serovar Typhi cause systemic infection in humans with typhoidal symptoms.
source: S. enterica serovar Typhi cause systemic infection in humans with typhoidal symptoms.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Salmonella Typhi.

claim: Recent reports reported incidences of 21 million typhoid cases round the year.
source: Recent reports reported incidences of 21 million (Bhutta, 2009) typhoid cases and 93 million of non-typhoidal (Majowicz et al., 2010) cases round the year.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bhutta, 2009.

claim: Recent reports reported incidences of 93 million non-typhoidal cases round the year.
source: Recent reports reported incidences of 21 million (Bhutta, 2009) typhoid cases and 93 million of non-typhoidal (Majowicz et al., 2010) cases round the year.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Majowicz et al., 2010.

claim: The virulence of Salmonella is majorly regulated by two pathogenicity islands, namely, SPI-1 and SPI-2.
source: The virulence of Salmonella is majorly regulated by two pathogenicity islands, namely, SPI-1 and SPI-2.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Salmonella virulence.

claim: Salmonella uses SPI-1 encoded T3SS and the effector proteins to invade host cells.
source: It uses SPI-1 encoded T3SS and the effector proteins to invade host cells (Haraga et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Haraga et al., 2008.

claim: Inside the macrophages, Salmonella harbour within the Salmonella containing vacuoles (SCV) by virtue of its SPI-2 effectors.
source: Inside the macrophages, they harbour within the Salmonella containing vacuoles (SCV) by virtue of its SPI-2 effectors (Hajra et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hajra et al., 2021.

claim: Macrophages, dendritic cells, and neutrophils are responsible for successful dissemination throughout the body through the reticulo-endothelial system (RES).
source: Macrophages, dendritic cells, and neutrophils are responsible for successful dissemination throughout the body through the reticulo-endothelial system (RES) (Haraga et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Haraga et al., 2008.

claim: M1 macrophages comprise of the proinflammatory antimicrobial state producing IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-12, and IFN-γ cytokines and exhibit enhanced expression of CD80, CD86 surface markers.
source: M1 macrophages comprise of the proinflammatory antimicrobial state producing IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-12, and IFN-γ cytokines and exhibit enhanced expression of CD80, CD86 surface markers.
evidence: This is established knowledge about M1 macrophage characteristics.

claim: The anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages promote bacterial persistence by producing anti-inflammatory cytokines like IL-10 and TGF-β and show increased expression of Arg-1 and CD206 surface markers.
source: The anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages promote bacterial persistence by producing anti-inflammatory cytokines like IL-10 and TGF-β and show increased expression of Arg-1 and CD206 surface markers (Lawrence and Natoli, 2011; Martinez et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lawrence and Natoli, 2011; Martinez et al., 2009.

claim: M1 macrophages rely on glycolysis for their energy requirements.
source: To sustain the continuous production of proinflammatory cytokines, M1 macrophages rely on glycolysis for their energy requirements.
evidence: This is established knowledge about M1 macrophage metabolism.

claim: M2 macrophages are fuelled by enhanced oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and FAO.
source: On the other hand, M2 macrophages are fuelled by enhanced oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and FAO (Namgaladze and Brüne, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Namgaladze and Brüne, 2014.

claim: SIRT1 has the ability to promote the polarization of M2 macrophages and inhibit inflammation in macrophages of adipose tissue.
source: SIRT1 has the ability to promote the polarization of M2 macrophages and inhibit inflammation in macrophages of adipose tissue (Hui et al., 2017; Jia et al., 2017; Kratz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hui et al., 2017; Jia et al., 2017; Kratz et al., 2014.

claim: SIRT3 suppresses ROS by deacetylating and activating MnSOD.
source: SIRT3 suppresses ROS by deacetylating and activating MnSOD (Cimen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cimen et al., 2010.

claim: Salmonella Typhimurium uses its SPI-2 effectors to inhibit the recruitment of NADPH oxidase to the SCV, thereby preventing oxidative burst-mediated microbicidal activity.
source: Salmonella Typhimurium uses its SPI-2 effectors to inhibit the recruitment of NADPH oxidase to the SCV, thereby preventing oxidative burst-mediated microbicidal activity (Vazquez-Torres et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vazquez-Torres et al., 2000.

claim: Mycobacterium bovis bacillus Calmette–Guérin prevents NOS2 recruitment to phagosomes.
source: Similarly, Mycobacterium bovis bacillus Calmette–Guérin prevents NOS2 recruitment to phagosomes (Miller et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Miller et al., 2004.

claim: Salmonella Dublin causes inhibition of the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines like IL-18 and IL-12p70.
source: Salmonella Dublin causes inhibition of the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines like IL-18 and IL-12p70 (Bost and Clements, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bost and Clements, 1997.

claim: Mycobacteria inhibits NFκB signalling and IFN-γ-mediated downstream pathways.
source: Moreover, Mycobacteria inhibits NFκB signalling and IFN-γ-mediated downstream pathways (Pathak et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pathak et al., 2007.

claim: Yersinia enterocolitica elicits an M2 response by inducing arginase-1 expression and TGF-β1 and IL-4 production.
source: Furthermore, Yersinia enterocolitica elicits an M2 response by inducing arginase-1 expression and TGF-β1 and IL-4 production (Tumitan et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tumitan et al., 2007.

claim: Yersinia TTSS effector LcrV induces an M2 phenotype supposedly by IL-10 production.
source: Yersinia TTSS effector LcrV induces an M2 phenotype supposedly by IL-10 production (Brubaker, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brubaker, 2003.

claim: Upon infection of RAW 264.7 murine macrophages with wildtype S. Typhimurium strain 14028S, an increased expression level of Sirt1 and Sirt3 was observed at initial and middle phases of infection, precisely at 2 hr and 6 hr post-infection through qPCR.
source: Upon infection of RAW 264.7 murine macrophages with wildtype S. Typhimurium strain 14028S, we observed an increased expression level of Sirt1 and Sirt3 at initial and middle phases of infection, precisely at 2 hr and 6 hr post-infection through qPCR (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: The Sirt1 expression level declined at later phases of infection.
source: The Sirt1 expression level declined at later phases of infection.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the qPCR results.

claim: The Sirt3 transcript levels remained elevated at all time points with respect to uninfected control with a marked increment at 16 hr time point post-infection, which subsided at 20 hr post-infection.
source: On the other hand, the Sirt3 transcript levels remained elevated at all time points with respect to uninfected control with a marked increment at 16 hr time point post-infection, which subsided at 20 hr post-infection.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the qPCR results.

claim: The expression profile of Sirt1 and Sirt3 in primary macrophages like peritoneal macrophages of C57BL/6 mice showed a similar trend of elevated expression at initial (2 hr), middle (6 hr), and late (16 hr) time points post-infection.
source: We even monitored the expression profile of Sirt1 and Sirt3 in primary macrophages like peritoneal macrophages of C57BL/6 mice and observed a similar trend of elevated expression at initial (2 hr), middle (6 hr), and late (16 hr) time points post-infection (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: In confocal laser scanning microscopy (CSLM) studies, an increase in SIRT1 and SIRT3 expression was observed at 6 hr post-infection within the infected RAW 264.7 macrophages.
source: In confocal laser scanning microscopy (CSLM) studies, we observed a similar increase in SIRT1 and SIRT3 expression at 6 hr post-infection within the infected macrophages RAW 264.7 macrophages. (Figure 1E–H).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1E-H.

claim: Immunoblotting revealed increased protein expression of both SIRT1 and SIRT3 at 2 hr post-infection in comparison to the uninfected control.
source: Immunoblotting revealed increased protein expression of both SIRT1 and SIRT3 at 2 hr post-infection in comparison to the uninfected control (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: SIRT1 expression exhibits a gradual decline at the late phase of infection.
source: However, SIRT1 expression exhibits a gradual decline at the late phase of infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and C.

claim: SIRT3 immunoblotting data shows an increased protein expression profile at 6 hr and 16 hr post-infection.
source: In line with the confocal microscopy data, SIRT3 immunoblotting data shows an increased protein expression profile at 6 hr and 16 hr post-infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: Wildtype S. Typhimurium can induce the expression of both SIRT1 and SIRT3 within the infected RAW 264.7 macrophages.
source: Our results depict the ability of wildtype S. Typhimurium to induce the expression of both SIRT1 and SIRT3 within the infected RAW 264.7 macrophages.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the results of infection with wildtype and mutant strains.

claim: Infection with either SPI-1 or SPI-2 mutant abrogates the induction of Sirt1.
source: However, infection with either SPI-1 or SPI-2 mutant abrogates the induction of Sirt1, whereas only SPI-2 mutants (∆ssaV and ∆steE) and not SPI-1 mutant infection caused reduction in Sirt3 transcript-level expression in the infected macrophages, implicating the role of SPI-1 and SPI-2 genes in triggering SIRT1 and SIRT3 in the infected macrophages (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1I and J.

claim: Only SPI-2 mutants (∆ssaV and ∆steE) and not SPI-1 mutant infection caused reduction in Sirt3 transcript-level expression in the infected macrophages.
source: However, infection with either SPI-1 or SPI-2 mutant abrogates the induction of Sirt1, whereas only SPI-2 mutants (∆ssaV and ∆steE) and not SPI-1 mutant infection caused reduction in Sirt3 transcript-level expression in the infected macrophages, implicating the role of SPI-1 and SPI-2 genes in triggering SIRT1 and SIRT3 in the infected macrophages (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1I and J.

claim: At the protein level, only SPI-2 mutant infection resulted in a predominant decline in SIRT3 expression and a mild reduction in SIRT1 expression.
source: However, at the protein level, only SPI-2 mutant infection resulted in a predominant decline in SIRT3 expression and a mild reduction in SIRT1 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There was a 20-fold and 5-fold increase in Sirt1 and Sirt3 expression in M2-polarized-infected macrophages at 16 hr post-infection.
source: Further, we examined the transcript-level profile of Sirt1 and Sirt3 in M1 or M2 polarized RAW 264.7 macrophages at 16 hr post-infection and observed 20-fold and 5-fold increase in Sirt1 and Sirt3 expression in M2-polarized-infected macrophages as opposed to 0.5-fold and 0.4-fold downregulation in M1-polarized-infected macrophages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: There was a 0.5-fold and 0.4-fold downregulation in Sirt1 and Sirt3 expression in M1-polarized-infected macrophages at 16 hr post-infection.
source: Further, we examined the transcript-level profile of Sirt1 and Sirt3 in M1 or M2 polarized RAW 264.7 macrophages at 16 hr post-infection and observed 20-fold and 5-fold increase in Sirt1 and Sirt3 expression in M2-polarized-infected macrophages as opposed to 0.5-fold and 0.4-fold downregulation in M1-polarized-infected macrophages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: S. Typhimurium exhibited increased intracellular fold proliferation within anti-inflammatory M2-polarized macrophages in comparison to the pro-inflammatory M1-polarized RAW 264.7 macrophages.
source: S. Typhimurium exhibited increased intracellular fold proliferation within anti-inflammatory M2-polarized macrophages in comparison to the pro-inflammatory M1-polarized RAW 264.7 macrophages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by intracellular proliferation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: Salmonella exhibits compromised intracellular survival in Sirt1 and Sirt3 knockdown RAW 264.7 macrophages in comparison to the untransfected and scrambled controls.
source: Salmonella exhibits compromised intracellular survival in Sirt1 and Sirt3 knockdown RAW 264.7 macrophages in comparison to the untransfected and scrambled controls (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by gentamicin protection assay data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: SIRT1 or SIRT3 inhibitor-treated peritoneal macrophages exhibited attenuated intracellular replication in comparison to the untreated peritoneal macrophages.
source: Further, we have assessed the intracellular proliferation in peritoneal macrophages isolated from thioglycolate-treated adult C57BL/6 mice post SIRT1 (EX-527) and SIRT3 (3TYP) inhibitor treatment. SIRT1 or SIRT3 inhibitor-treated macrophages exhibited attenuated intracellular replication in comparison to the untreated peritoneal macrophages (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by intracellular proliferation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Inhibition of both SIRT1 and SIRT3 increased production of pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-6 significantly at 2 hr and 20 hr post-infection.
source: Inhibition of both SIRT1 and SIRT3 increased production of pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-6 significantly at 2 hr and 20 hr post-infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There was only a significant reduction in anti-inflammatory IL-10 production upon Sirt1 and Sirt3 knockdown at 2 hr and 20 hr post-infection.
source: Moreover, there was only a significant reduction in anti-inflammatory IL-10 production upon Sirt1 and Sirt3 knockdown at 2 hr and 20 hr post-infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In peritoneal macrophages upon SIRT1 (EX-527-1 µM) or SIRT3 (3-TYP-1µM) chemical inhibitor treatment, an increase in IL-6 and IL-1β cytokine levels was observed at 6 hr post-infection.
source: In peritoneal macrophages upon SIRT1 (EX-527-1 µM) or SIRT3 (3-TYP-1µM) chemical inhibitor treatment, an increase in IL-6 and IL-1β cytokine levels was observed at 6 hr post-infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: Along the course of infection, there was a reduction in the expression of M1 markers like Nos2, Cd40,Cd86, Tnfa, Nfkb2, Il6 and a corresponding increase in the expression of the M2 markers such as Arg1, Ccl17, Cd206, IL4ra with an exception of Tgfb.
source: Along the course of infection, there was a reduction in the expression of M1 markers like Nos2, Cd40,Cd86, Tnfa, Nfkb2, Il6 and a corresponding increase in the expression of the M2 markers such as Arg1, Ccl17, Cd206, IL4ra with an exception of Tgfb (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by nanoString gene expression data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The data suggests a distinct decrease in CD86-positive population in the infected sets in comparison to the uninfected and the fixed dead bacteria control along the course of S. Typhimurium infection.
source: The data suggests a distinct decrease in CD86-positive population in the infected sets in comparison to the uninfected and the fixed dead bacteria control along the course of S. Typhimurium infection (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Knockdown of Sirt1 or Sirt3 in infected RAW 264.7 macrophages resulted in a reduction in anti-inflammatory CD206 surface marker expression at 16 hr post-infection.
source: Knockdown of Sirt1 or Sirt3 in infected RAW 264.7 macrophages resulted in a reduction in anti-inflammatory CD206 surface marker expression at 16 hr post-infection (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Sirt1 or Sirt3 knockdown led to enhanced intracellular ROS generation within the infected macrophages in comparison to the scrambled or the untransfected control.
source: Moreover, Sirt1 or Sirt3 knockdown led to enhanced intracellular ROS generation within the infected macrophages in comparison to the scrambled or the untransfected control (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by DCFDA staining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The haematoxylin and eosin staining of the S. Typhimurium-infected mice liver tissue sections depicted exacerbated signs of inflammation in the SIRT1 (EX-527) or SIRT3 (3TYP) inhibitor-treated cohorts in comparison to the untreated controls with multiple necrotic foci and increased influx of inflammatory cell inflates.
source: Further, the haematoxylin and eosin staining of the S. Typhimurium-infected mice liver tissue sections depicted exacerbated signs of inflammation in the SIRT1 (EX-527) or SIRT3 (3TYP) inhibitor-treated cohorts in comparison to the untreated controls with multiple necrotic foci and increased influx of inflammatory cell inflates.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the histological analysis.

claim: These acute inflammatory signs of the liver sections get ameliorated in the SIRT1 (SRT1720) activator-treated infected cohort.
source: Moreover, these acute inflammatory signs of the liver sections get ameliorated in the SIRT1 (SRT1720) activator-treated infected cohort.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the histological analysis.

claim: An increased interaction of SIRT1 with NF-κB p65 was observed in the infected macrophages in comparison to the uninfected control.
source: We observed an increased interaction of SIRT1 with NF-κB p65 in the infected macrophages in comparison to the uninfected control (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The knockdown of Sirt1 resulted in increased acetylation status of the NF-κB p65 upon infection in comparison to the scrambled, infected control.
source: Further, the knockdown of Sirt1 resulted in increased acetylation status of the NF-κB p65 upon infection in comparison to the scrambled, infected control (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: An increased interaction of NF-κB p65 with SIRT1 was observed in the infected untreated macrophages compared to the untreated uninfected control.
source: We observed an increased interaction of NF-κB p65 with SIRT1 in the infected untreated macrophages compared to the untreated uninfected control (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The interaction of NF-κB p65 with SIRT1 gets abrogated under the EX-527 inhibitor treatment in the infected macrophages, thereby implying the function of the catalytic domain in mediating the interaction.
source: However, the interaction of NF-κB p65 with SIRT1 gets abrogated under the EX-527 inhibitor treatment in the infected macrophages, thereby implying the function of the catalytic domain in mediating the interaction (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: An increased acetylation status of NF-κB p65 was observed in the EX-527-treated infected macrophages in comparison to the untreated infected macrophages.
source: Moreover, an increased acetylation status of NF-κB p65 was observed in the EX-527-treated infected macrophages in comparison to the untreated infected macrophages (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Results depicted significant enhancement in the production of ROS at 16 hr post-infection upon knockdown of Sirt1 or Sirt3 in comparison to untransfected or scrambled control.
source: Results depicted significant enhancement in the production of ROS at 16 hr post-infection upon knockdown of Sirt1 or Sirt3 in comparison to untransfected or scrambled control (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by DCFDA staining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: Higher ROS generation was detected upon Sirt3 KD at 6 hr post-infection and greater ROS production at 16 hr and 20 hr time points in Sirt1 knockdown macrophages.
source: Upon detection of extracellular ROS generation through phenol red hydrogen peroxidase assay, we detected higher ROS generation upon Sirt3 KD at 6 hr post-infection and greater ROS production at 16 hr and 20 hr time points in Sirt1 knockdown macrophages (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by phenol red hydrogen peroxidase assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The attenuated intracellular proliferation of S. Typhimurium within the knockdown or the chemical inhibitor-treated macrophages got restored upon 1 mM treatment of ROS scavenger, NAC.
source: The attenuated intracellular proliferation of S. Typhimurium within the knockdown or the chemical inhibitor-treated macrophages got restored upon 1 mM treatment of ROS scavenger, NAC (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by intracellular proliferation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Analysis of the gene profile revealed upregulation of genes involved in FAO and tricarboxylic acid cycle and corresponding downregulation of genes involved in glycolysis.
source: Analysis of the gene profile revealed upregulation of genes involved in FAO and tricarboxylic acid cycle and corresponding downregulation of genes involved in glycolysis (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by nanoString gene expression data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The mRNA level of Pppard was elevated to twofold at 2 hr and 6 hr post-infection and around sixfold upregulation in mRNA transcript was noted at 16 hr post-infection.
source: We found that the mRNA level was elevated to twofold at 2 hr and 6 hr post-infection. At the late phase of infection, 16 hr post-infection around sixfold upregulation in mRNA transcript was noted (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Lactate estimation assay of S. Typhimurium-infected RAW 264.7 macrophages at the initial time point of 2 hr and at the late time point of 16 hr post-infection revealed a decline in lactate (glycolysis end product) production at 16 hr in comparison to 2 hr post-infection time point.
source: Lactate estimation assay of S. Typhimurium-infected RAW 264.7 macrophages at the initial time point of 2 hr and at the late time point of 16 hr post-infection revealed a decline in lactate (glycolysis end product) production at 16 hr in comparison to 2 hr post-infection time point (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by lactate estimation assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Lactate estimation assay in Sirt1 and Sirt3 knockdown condition revealed enhanced lactate production at 16 hr post-infection in comparison to the scrambled control.
source: Lactate estimation assay in Sirt1 and Sirt3 knockdown condition revealed enhanced lactate production at 16 hr post-infection in comparison to the scrambled control, which further authenticates the increased host glycolysis upon Sirt1 and Sirt3 knockdown scenario (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is supported by lactate estimation assay data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: Sirt1 and Sirt3 knockdown RAW 264.7-infected macrophages showed decreased expression of fatty acid oxidizing genes and increased expression of glycolytic Pfkl gene in comparison to the scrambled infected control.
source: Sirt1 and Sirt3 knockdown RAW 264.7-infected macrophages showed decreased expression of fatty acid oxidizing genes and increased expression of glycolytic Pfkl gene in comparison to the scrambled infected control (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Similar results were obtained in the infected peritoneal macrophages under the SIRT1 or SIRT3 catalytic inhibitor treatment.
source: Similar results were obtained in the infected peritoneal macrophages under the SIRT1 or SIRT3 catalytic inhibitor treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: qRT PCR-mediated metabolic gene profiling of liver and spleen isolated from wildtype S. Typhimurium-infected macrophages revealed decreased transcript-level expression of murine FAO genes upon treatment with SIRT1 (EX-527) or SIRT3 (3TYP) catalytic inhibitors, which got reversed upon SIRT1 activator (SRT1720) treatment.
source: Moreover, qRT PCR-mediated metabolic gene profiling of liver and spleen isolated from wildtype S. Typhimurium-infected macrophages revealed decreased transcript-level expression of murine FAO genes upon treatment with SIRT1 (EX-527) or SIRT3 (3TYP) catalytic inhibitors, which got reversed upon SIRT1 activator (SRT1720) treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: SIRT1 and SIRT3 knockdown or catalytic inhibition in peritoneal macrophages resulted in increased protein expression of host glycolytic genes such as phosphoglycerate kinase (Pgk), phosphofructokinase (Pfk) with concomitant reduction in protein expression of TCA cycle gene like pyruvate dehydrogenase (Pdha1) and FAO genes such as Hadha and Acox1.
source: Moreover, SIRT1 and SIRT3 knockdown or catalytic inhibition in peritoneal macrophages resulted in increased protein expression of host glycolytic genes such as phosphoglycerate kinase (Pgk), phosphofructokinase (Pfk) with concomitant reduction in protein expression of TCA cycle gene like pyruvate dehydrogenase (Pdha1) and FAO genes such as Hadha and Acox1 (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.
